definition: Corollary means a natural or direct consequence that follows automatically from something else.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word corollary. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know corollary should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: When the factory added a night shift, the corollary was a sudden demand for late-running buses.
An aftereffect is anything that lingers once an event is over, while a corollary follows logically and predictably from it.
A corollary follows naturally from a first fact, but an inevitability is even stronger: an outcome that absolutely cannot be avoided.

A consequence is any result that follows from an action or condition — good or bad, expected or not. A corollary is a special kind of consequence: one that follows naturally and automatically once the first fact is in place, with no extra push needed. Every corollary is a consequence, but only the automatic, logical ones earn the name corollary.

An outgrowth is something that develops gradually out of something else, the way a weekend hobby becomes a business. A corollary follows more tightly and predictably: state the first fact and the corollary comes with it. An outgrowth needs time to grow; a corollary is already implied.

Corollary means a natural or direct consequence that follows automatically from something else.
A small island town finally got high-speed internet, and remote workers began moving in by the dozen.
The newcomers brought welcome income to shops and cafes.
But a corollary soon followed: with more people bidding on the same few houses, rents climbed beyond what many longtime residents could pay.
No one had planned the rent spike; it flowed naturally from the arrival of the new workers.
The rent increase was not a separate accident; it followed naturally and automatically from the influx of new residents, which is exactly what a corollary is.
Corollary usually appears as 'a corollary of' or 'a corollary to' a first fact or decision (a corollary of the new policy).
It names what follows naturally and automatically once something else is true; it is not the cause of that thing, and not a result someone deliberately engineered.

corollary: A corollary follows naturally from a first fact, but an inevitability is even stronger: an outcome that absolutely cannot be avoided.
When the principal announced that lunch would grow by fifteen minutes, the cafeteria cheered.
The vice principal, standing beside her with the master schedule, did not.
He saw the corollary at once: the school day was fixed, so a longer lunch meant every passing period shrank the moment the plan was stated.
No one had to decide anything further, and nothing needed time to develop -- the crowded hallways were already contained in the announcement, the way a shadow comes with a lamppost.
By Friday, students who had cheered the lunch were writing petitions about the hallways, startled to learn that the two were one decision, not two.
